advances: Ordinary convex-body caps with a specified through-mark law, not a bound for the locked mixed-integer target. The complementary identity gives an upper bound on the captured fraction.

proof:
If the normal-marginal hypothesis holds, Gauss–Green for $x-g$ on each $D_j$ gives $d|D_j|$ as the integral of $h_{B-g}(n)$ over its retained old boundary with its outer normals $n$. The cut face contributes zero, and the intersection of the proper cut plane with the old boundary has $(d-1)$-measure zero. Summation against $\theta_j$ gives $\beta\int h_{B-g}\,dS_B=\beta d|B|$ by Gauss–Green on $B$.

A point of $B$ maximizing $u_j\cdot(x-g)$ and the whole actual section $F_j$ form a pyramid inside $D_j$, of volume $s_jh_j^+/d$. This proves $e_j^+\ge0$ and shows that it does not depend on the choice of farthest apex. The complement up to a null plane is the closed opposite cap; the analogous pyramid gives $e_j^-\ge0$. Summation gives the two identities with the indicated support integrals. If $R=S_J$, the standard surface-area formula $V(J[d-1],B)=\int h_{B-g}(v)\,dS_J(v)/d$ gives the negative-side integral. Reflection of $J$ turns this into the positive-side integral; translation of $B$ does not affect the mixed volume.

For the captured side, equality means that every nonnegative remainder vanishes, because all weights are positive. Each pyramid is a full-dimensional compact convex subset of its cap. If such a subset is proper, a point of the cap outside it has positive distance from it; by moving slightly toward an interior point of the cap one obtains an interior ball outside the subset, showing strict volume loss. Thus zero remainder means equality of the sets. Minkowski's first inequality for the pair $(-J,B)$ gives $\alpha(B,J)\ge1$, with equality for homothetic bodies only. This proves the final comparison.
statement:
Let $B\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a convex body, $d\ge2$, $g\in\operatorname{int}B$, and let finitely many positive weights $\theta_j$ sum to one. For unit $u_j$ set $D_j=B\cap\{x:u_j\cdot(x-g)\ge0\}$, let $F_j$ be the cut section with $(d-1)$-area $s_j$, and write $h_j^\pm=h_{B-g}(\pm u_j)$. Suppose $\sum_j\theta_j|D_j|=\beta|B|$; this holds if the weighted original-boundary normal marginal of these caps is $\beta S_B$. Set $R=\sum_j\theta_js_j\delta_{-u_j}$ and $e_j^+=|D_j|-s_jh_j^+/d$, $e_j^-=|B\setminus D_j|-s_jh_j^-/d$. Both remainders are nonnegative. If $R=S_J$ for a positive convex body $J$, then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta|B|&=V((-J)[d-1],B)+\sum_j\theta_je_j^+,\\
(1-\beta)|B|&=V(J[d-1],B)+\sum_j\theta_je_j^-.
\end{aligned}
$$
Without $J$ the two mixed volumes are respectively the integrals of $h_{B-g}(-v)$ and $h_{B-g}(v)$ against $R/d$. Equality in the captured-cap lower bound holds precisely when each $D_j$ equals the pyramid over $F_j$ with a farthest captured apex. For $R=S_J$,
$$
\beta\ge\alpha(B,J)(|J|/|B|)^{(d-1)/d}\ge (|J|/|B|)^{(d-1)/d},\qquad
\alpha(B,J)=\frac{V((-J)[d-1],B)}{|J|^{(d-1)/d}|B|^{1/d}}.
$$
Equality in the final volume lower bound also requires $-J$ and $B$ to be homothetic.
title: Oriented mixed-volume bounds with exact actual cap pyramid remainders
